Neonatal Nurse sharks emerge from their mothers at approximately 28 cm [Lb = approximately 28 cm] in total length, a size that facilitates independent foraging soon after parturition. This species employs a yolk-sac viviparous reproductive strategy, and following a gestation period of 5 to 6 months at typical water temperatures around 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the developing young achieve an age at birth of approximately 167.75 days [ab = approximately 167.75 days]. The neonates immediately commence feeding on benthic invertebrates and small fishes, transitioning rapidly from yolk absorption to active prey detection. The initial growth phase is relatively rapid, as these young individuals double their length within their first few years, gradually shifting their diet to include crustaceans and mollusks. The extended developmental period in utero ensures that each pup possesses a well-developed yolk sac, providing substantial nutritional reserves for the first weeks of exotrophic life. Observations from field studies in Caribbean nurseries indicate that the onset of independent foraging, typically occurring within days of birth, is a critical survival bottleneck, with mortality rates highest during this initial transition.

Female Nurse sharks attain sexual maturation at a total length of approximately 235 cm [Lp = approximately 235 cm], a milestone that generally occurs when individuals are between 27 and 30 years of age. This delayed onset of puberty is characteristic of slow-growing, long-lived elasmobranchs and reflects the substantial energetic investment required to reach a sufficiently large body size for successful reproduction. Upon reaching this length, females begin to exhibit the capacity for clasper-mediated fertilisation, undergoing ovarian maturation and initiating vitellogenesis. The total length at puberty is notably smaller than the ultimate total length for females (430 cm) [Li = 430 cm], which exceeds four meters, indicating an extended post-pubertal growth period during which the somatic growth continues alongside reproductive activity. This continued growth is facilitated by a diet increasingly dominated by larger prey items, including stingrays, sea urchins, and teleost fishes. The disparity between size at maturity and maximum size suggests that females gain significant fitness benefits from further growth, likely through increased fecundity and improved competitive ability within the social hierarchy of resting aggregations. Tracking studies have confirmed that mature females regularly return to specific pupping grounds along the Caribbean coast.

Under thermal conditions characteristic of their tropical and subtropical habitat, approximately 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the maximum reproductive rate for Nurse sharks involves a single litter produced each year [F_R_i = single litter produced each year]. Each gravid female typically carries between 21 and 28 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 21 and 28 pups per litter], making this one of the larger litter sizes recorded among orectolobiform sharks. The combination of a single annual litter with such a substantial number of offspring represents a relatively high annual reproductive output for a large-bodied elasmobranch. The reproductive cycle is biennial in some populations, with ovulation, copulation, and sperm storage preceding the internal fertilisation that follows the female's return to optimal foraging grounds. During the lengthy gestation, the uterine embryos rely initially on yolk reserves before transitioning to a form of histotrophy, in which the female secretes nutrient-rich uterine fluid. This matrotrophic support allows the developing embryos to nearly double in length within the uterus. Post-parturition, the female typically enters a period of reproductive quiescence before the next gametogenesis onset.

The maximum documented lifespan for the Nurse shark, recorded under field conditions at a mean annual water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], extends to approximately 9125 days [am = approximately 9125 days], or roughly 25 years. This longevity, combined with a late age at puberty, places the Nurse shark firmly within the category of slow life-history strategists, with a generation time that exceeds fifteen years. Senescence in this species appears gradual, with oldest individuals showing reduced reproductive output and increased susceptibility to parasitic infections. Studies of growth bands in vertebral centra have validated that individuals reaching this maximum age exhibit slowed somatic growth, with females attaining the species' characteristic ultimate total length of approximately 430 cm [Li = approximately 430 cm] only after several decades of life. This asymptotic length is rarely observed in the wild, suggesting that most individuals do not survive to fully realize their growth potential. The physiological death of these mature elasmobranchs is often preceded by a period of declining body condition, marked by the depletion of lipid stores and reduced feeding activity. Population models indicate that the species' low natural adult mortality is crucial for maintaining stable populations despite the protracted pre-reproductive period.

A comparison of the life-history parameters of Ginglymostoma cirratum with those of other orectolobiform sharks reveals a clear pattern of slow growth and late maturation, even by elasmobranch standards. The total length at birth of approximately 28 cm [Lb = approximately 28 cm] is modest relative to the maximum size, suggesting that neonates are born at a relatively undeveloped stage compared to some viviparous species, and this early size may influence their reliance on shallow, structurally complex nursery habitats that offer refuge from predators. The age at birth of around 5.5 months [ab = around 5.5 months], when considered at the population's average thermal regime of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], falls within the typical range for tropical aplacental viviparous elasmobranchs. A key demographic parameter is the total length at puberty for females, approximately 235 cm [Lp = approximately 235 cm], which represents just over half of the ultimate total length (430 cm) [Li = 430 cm], a proportion consistent with other long-lived sharks. Annual reproductive output, with a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] yielding 21 to 28 pups per litter [N_R_i = 21 to 28 pups per litter], is considerable. The species' maximum lifespan of 25 years [am = 25 years] is moderate compared to larger laminiforms but substantial relative to its body size, reinforcing the evolutionary trade-off between delayed reproduction and extended longevity in stable, low-mortality environments at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C].
